messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan's eyes still widened when he recalled the sound of screeching tires and crunching metal. It had been two years since the car accident that took his wife's life, but the memory remained as vivid as ever. He couldn't find the words to describe the horror of watching her slip away, and even now, recalling it brought back the same terror he felt in those moments. It was a fear that lingered long after the funeral, when strangers would offer condolences or talk about their own losses. Rohan would tense up, his mind flashing back to the scene of the accident. Cars passing by on the road outside his home seemed to hit him like a punch to the gut, and he'd find himself scanning the surroundings for signs of danger. Talking to strangers made him feel uneasy; he couldn't shake off the feeling that people were not what they seemed. As a fisherman, Rohan was no stranger to the quiet rhythms of the sea. But after the accident, unusual silences began to unsettle him – an unspoken threat lurking beneath the surface. He'd find himself on high alert even inside his own home, expecting something to go terribly wrong at any moment. His body felt like a liability, prone to betraying him when he needed it most. Rohan couldn't help but wonder if this was what people meant by "identity loss." He used to be the man who could navigate treacherous waters with ease; now, even walking down the street made him feel like an imposter. The more he struggled to trust himself, the more his surroundings seemed to confirm his fears. People's faces blurred together into a sea of potential threats. At home, Rohan would try to distract himself by watching TV or listening to music. But during quiet moments, his mind would drift back to that terrible day – the screech of tires, the shattering glass, and the feeling of utter powerlessness. His body would tighten, bracing for impact all over again. He couldn't shake off the conviction that the world was a minefield waiting to explode. One evening, while preparing dinner, Rohan caught himself staring at a stranger on TV – someone discussing their own loss. Before he knew it, his mind had transported him back to the scene of the accident. He felt like he was reliving those moments all over again. It was as if the memories were trying to tell him something – that danger lurked around every corner, waiting to strike. Rohan's anxiety reached a boiling point when a neighbor stopped by for an impromptu chat. As they talked about nothing in particular, Rohan found himself glancing nervously at the road outside. Cars passing by seemed more menacing than ever before. When his neighbor departed, Rohan locked the door behind him, feeling like he'd narrowly escaped some unspoken threat. In that moment, he realized he couldn't keep living this way – perpetually on edge, forever trapped in a world of silent terrors and unseen dangers. It was time to confront these fears head-on, no matter how daunting the prospect seemed.
